sources.title: RIT CSCI-632 Mobile Robot Programming catalog description
sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.content: This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

sources.title: OpenCV Documentation
sources.author: OpenCV
sources.content: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare Advances in Computer Vision
sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.content: Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.
